summary: Gives an overview of applications expected to run on a Quantum Internet and groups them into categories. It also discusses some general requirements for the Quantum Internet, aiming to describe a framework for applications and the needs they place on the network. It is informational.

plainLanguage.summary: A quantum internet would link special computers in new ways. This describes what people might do with it, like secret messages.

subtitle: Vision for quantum network applications including cryptography, sensing and computing

tldr.problem: As quantum technology advances, the question arises: what will a Quantum Internet enable? How will it fit into the existing Internet? What requirements will it place on networks?
tldr.mechanism: This RFC catalogs expected applications for a future Quantum Internet, groups them by purpose, and explores three detailed scenarios: secure key distribution, blind quantum computing, and distributed quantum computing. It then maps these to stages of quantum technology development and identifies networking requirements.
tldr.outcome: A framework for understanding what a Quantum Internet might do and how it will need to work, guiding research and standardization efforts.

today: RFC 9583 is an Informational document representing the consensus of the Quantum Internet Research Group. It has not been obsoleted or updated. It remains a foundational roadmap document for quantum internet development, describing the applications researchers aim to enable and the architectural requirements those applications impose on emerging quantum networks.

sections.title: Introduction to the Quantum Internet
sections.content:
The Classical Internet, the Internet we use today, carries classical bits: sequences of 0s and 1s. A Quantum Internet will augment it with quantum channels and nodes that process qubits (quantum bits).

Unlike a classical bit, a qubit can exist in a superposition of 0 and 1 before measurement. Qubits also exhibit entanglement: a correlation between distant qubits that has no classical counterpart. These quantum properties enable new applications for security, computing and sensing.

The Quantum Internet is not intended to replace the Classical Internet. Instead, it will work alongside it, enhancing security, speeding up computation, and enabling new capabilities. This document, produced by the Quantum Internet Research Group, surveys the applications expected to run on a Quantum Internet and the requirements they place on the network.
sections.plainLanguage: A quantum internet is a new kind of network being built with quantum computers. Instead of sending 0s and 1s like regular internet, it sends quantum bits that can be 0 and 1 at the same time in strange ways.

sections.title: Three Categories of Quantum Applications
sections.content:
Quantum Cryptography uses quantum properties to secure communication. The most mature application is Quantum Key Distribution (QKD), which lets two parties create a shared secret key with information-theoretic security: unbreakable even against a quantum computer. Other quantum cryptography applications include quantum money (exploiting the no-cloning property of unknown quantum states) and fast Byzantine agreement (using entanglement to speed consensus protocols).

Quantum Sensing and Metrology use entanglement and superposition to measure physical quantities with precision beyond what classical sensors can achieve. Applications include ultra-precise network clock synchronization (synchronized across multiple distant sites), high-sensitivity nanoscale sensing, and quantum-enhanced astronomical telescopes.

Quantum Computing harnesses quantum mechanics to solve certain computation problems exponentially faster than classical computers. On a Quantum Internet, distributed quantum computing connects multiple small quantum computers to work together as a virtual larger computer. Blind quantum computing lets a client delegate computation to a remote quantum computer while hiding the data being computed.
sections.plainLanguage: There are three main things the quantum internet could do: send secret codes that no one can crack, measure super tiny things more accurately than ever, and do calculations way faster than normal computers.

sections.title: Three Detailed Application Scenarios
sections.content:
Secure Communication Setup: Two quantum nodes use Quantum Key Distribution to establish a secret cryptographic key. In the BB84 QKD protocol (the first and most famous), one node encodes random bits into qubits using random bases, sends them to a second node, which measures each qubit in a random basis. Both nodes then publicly discuss which bases they used (not the results). The bits where their bases matched form the raw key. Post-processing on an authenticated classical channel removes errors and distills the final secret key. An eavesdropper trying to intercept the qubits would be detected because quantum measurement disturbs the state.

Blind Quantum Computing: A client with limited quantum capability delegates computation to a remote quantum server without revealing the computation or the data. The client transforms qubits before sending them; the server performs quantum gates on the transformed qubits; the server returns result qubits; the client transforms them back to get the answer. At each step, the server sees only transformed data, not the original problem.

Distributed Quantum Computing: Multiple small quantum computers (each with limited qubits) in different locations work together to solve a single large quantum computation. Qubits are teleported between sites using quantum teleportation: a process that uses a shared entangled pair and classical communication to transfer a qubit from one location to another. This enables cloud-style quantum computing where a user can leverage distributed NISQ (Noisy Intermediate-Scale Quantum) computers to solve complex problems like drug discovery.
sections.plainLanguage: Here are three things quantum internet could do: Alice and Bob swap secret codes in a way no hacker can peek. A client sends secret data to a server that solves it without seeing what the data is. Multiple weak quantum computers far apart team up to solve one hard problem together.

sections.title: Quantum Internet Development Stages
sections.content:
A Quantum Internet roadmap divides development into six stages, each enabling progressively more sophisticated applications:

Stage 1 (Trusted Repeater Networks): QKD over extended distances using trusted intermediate nodes that receive and re-transmit qubits. Limited end-to-end security because trusted nodes could be compromised.

Stage 2 (Prepare-and-Measure Networks): Quantum nodes can prepare and measure qubits. Enables prepare-and-measure QKD protocols and verification of classical passwords without revealing them.

Stage 3 (Entanglement Distribution Networks): Quantum repeaters distribute entangled Bell pairs across distances using entanglement swapping. Enables true end-to-end QKD without trusting intermediate nodes.

Stage 4 (Quantum Memory Networks): Quantum repeaters can store and manipulate qubits in quantum memories. Enables sophisticated applications like blind quantum computing, quantum secret sharing, and leader election.

Stage 5 (Fault-Tolerant Networks): Quantum repeaters perform error correction, enabling fault-tolerant quantum computation. Allows distributed quantum computing and quantum sensor applications.

Stage 6 (Quantum Computing Networks): Full-blown Quantum Internet with distributed quantum computing over many qubits.
sections.plainLanguage: The quantum internet will be built in stages. First just sending codes over distance, then measuring qubits, then sharing magic quantum pairs between far apart computers, then remembering qubits, then fixing errors, then full quantum computing.

sections.title: Networking Requirements
sections.content:
The Quantum Internet places four categories of requirements on the network:

Operations on Entangled Qubits: Applications need methods to trigger distribution of entangled pairs to any quantum nodes. This requires operations like entanglement swapping (where an intermediate node creates entanglement between two distant nodes) and entanglement distillation (improving the quality of entangled pairs).

Entanglement Distribution: Quantum repeaters and routers must support robust and efficient distribution of high-fidelity entangled pairs across distances. This means generating entangled pairs on each hop and performing entanglement swapping at intermediate nodes.

Classical Channels: Even though the Quantum Internet transfers qubits, it needs classical communication for control, coordination, and auxiliary information. QKD requires measurement results and basis information on a classical channel. Distributed quantum computing needs Bell measurement results sent classically between sites. Qubits lack packet headers, so routing and identification must travel classically.

Quantum Internet Management: Like any network, the Quantum Internet needs management and control: monitoring status, diagnosing problems, and configuring quantum nodes. This requires new management information models tailored to quantum resources like quantum memory, quantum channels and entangled connections.
sections.plainLanguage: The quantum network needs four things: ways to make entanglement happen between distant computers, ways to spread good entanglement far, regular radio communication to control things, and management tools to keep everything working.
